name: Ranking & Order — Positions in a Row
whatIsIt: Ranking puzzles tell you someone's position from two ends of a row or list and ask for the total, or ask a new rank after people join or leave. The master formula is: Total = (rank from top) + (rank from bottom) − 1. The '− 1' is because the person is counted once from each end.
whyNeeded: Ranking-and-order questions appear in almost every reasoning paper and are quick marks once you know the '+ minus one' rule. They also sharpen careful counting — the source of most silly errors.
realLifeUses: Reading class ranks and merit lists
Any 'how many in total' counting problem

vocabulary.meaning: Your position counting from the start/front (1st, 2nd…).
Your position counting from the end/back.
The error of counting the same person from both ends without subtracting 1.
How many people are in the row altogether.

story.title: Counted Twice, Subtract Once
story.text: Priya is 5th from the front and 8th from the back in a line. 'So the line has 5 + 8 = 13?' Her friend says 'Careful — YOU got counted from both ends, so you're counted twice. Subtract 1.' Total = 5 + 8 − 1 = 12. Priya nods: 'The person in the middle is shared, so minus one.' The rule sticks: add the two ranks, then subtract 1.
story.extractedProblem: Priya is 5th from front and 8th from back. How many in the line?
story.answerInStory: 12 — total = 5 + 8 − 1 = 12 (she is counted from both ends, so subtract 1).

visual.caption: 5th from front + 8th from back counts the same person twice. Total = 5 + 8 − 1 = 12.

teachingGallery.title: Add the two ranks, subtract 1
teachingGallery.note: Total = top rank + bottom rank − 1. The − 1 removes the person counted from both ends.

standardMethod.summary: Use Total = rank-from-top + rank-from-bottom − 1. To find a rank from the other end, rearrange: rank-from-bottom = Total − rank-from-top + 1.
steps: Identify the person's rank from the top and from the bottom.
Subtract 1 (the person is counted from both ends).
That is the total; to find one rank when you know the total, rearrange the same formula.

alternateMethods.name: Draw dots
alternateMethods.whenToUse: When you're unsure whether to subtract 1.
steps: Draw a small row of dots and mark the person.
Count from each end and see the shared dot in the middle.
The single shared dot is exactly why you subtract 1.

commonMistakes.mistake: Adding the two ranks and forgetting to subtract 1 (saying 5 + 8 = 13).
commonMistakes.fix: The person sits in BOTH counts, so they're counted twice. Always subtract 1: total = top + bottom − 1.

commonMistakes.mistake: Forgetting the + 1 when finding a rank from the other end.
commonMistakes.fix: Rearranged, the formula is rank-from-other-end = Total − rank + 1. The + 1 keeps it consistent with the − 1 rule.

teachBackPrompt: Teach a friend why 5th-from-front and 8th-from-back means 12 in the row, not 13. Use the 'counted from both ends, so subtract 1' idea and the formula Total = top + bottom − 1.

revisionCard.summary: Ranking & order: Total = rank-from-top + rank-from-bottom − 1 (the − 1 removes the person counted from both ends). To get a rank from the other end: rank = Total − known-rank + 1. When in doubt, draw dots and see the shared middle person. Watch the off-by-one on both formulas.

gameMission.title: Line-Up Logic
gameMission.brief: Work out how many animals are in the queue from two clues — add the ranks and never forget to subtract the one that's counted twice!

realLifeProject: Line up 6–8 friends. Pick one and have everyone verify: their rank from each end should add to (total + 1). Prove the formula with real people.

rememberIt.unpack: Total = top + bottom − 1; the shared person is counted from both ends.

studentQuestions.q: When do I add 1 and when do I subtract 1?
studentQuestions.a: Finding the TOTAL from two ranks → subtract 1. Finding a rank from the OTHER end when you know the total → Total − rank + 1 (add 1). They come from the same rule.

studentQuestions.q: What if people join or leave the line?
studentQuestions.a: Adjust the total first, then recompute. Draw the row if positions shift — a quick sketch prevents off-by-one mistakes.
